alt: Gas molecules moving randomly in a box. One molecule bounces off the right-hand wall and pushes on it with a force. Huge numbers of collisions every second give a steady force, and pressure is that force divided by the wall area.
caption: Pressure = the total force of molecules hitting a wall ÷ the area of the wall.

after: ## Absolute zero and the Kelvin scale (5.16, 5.17)
alt: Pressure against temperature in °C for a sealed flask: 100 kPa at 0 °C and 136.6 kPa at 100 °C. Extending the straight line back reaches zero pressure at −273 °C. The pressure rises 0.366 kPa per °C, and 100 ÷ 0.366 = 273.
caption: Extend the pressure–temperature line back to zero pressure: it always meets −273 °C.

after: ## Absolute zero and the Kelvin scale (5.16, 5.17)
alt: Two scales side by side: absolute zero is −273 °C and 0 K, water freezes at 0 °C and 273 K, room temperature is about 20 °C or 293 K, and water boils at 100 °C or 373 K.
caption: Add 273 to change °C to K; the steps are the same size.

after: ## Pressure and volume at constant temperature (5.20, 5.22)
alt: A bicycle pump with 150 cm³ of air at 100 kPa is pushed in slowly to 50 cm³; the molecules hit the walls more often and the pressure becomes 100 × 150 ÷ 50 = 300 kPa. A graph of p against V is a curve that gets less steep as V increases.
caption: One third of the volume, three times the pressure: p₁V₁ = p₂V₂.

after: ## Pressure and temperature at constant volume (5.20, 5.21)
alt: Two identical boxes of gas; in the hotter one the molecules move faster, so they hit the walls more often and harder and the pressure rises. Worked example: a tyre at 2.4 × 10⁵ Pa and 280 K heated to 310 K reaches 2.7 × 10⁵ Pa.
caption: Hotter means more frequent and harder collisions; use kelvin in p₁/T₁ = p₂/T₂.

alt: A 2.0 cm³ bubble released 20 m deep in fresh water, where the total pressure is 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa, rises to the surface at 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa. With p₁V₁ = p₂V₂ its volume becomes 6.0 cm³.
caption: Total pressure falls to a third, so the volume triples.
